submissions.findingTextShort: A 2024 meta-analysis found a modest maximal-intensity exercise signal for chronic beta-alanine supplementation in trained young men, with important duration and effort-context limits.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis included 18 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled studies and 331 trained male participants aged 18 to 40 years performing maximal or supramaximal efforts lasting 0.5 to 10 minutes. Chronic beta-alanine supplementation produced a modest pooled performance effect versus placebo, with subgroup signals varying by supplementation duration, daily dose, and effort duration. This evidence is specific to trained young men and maximal-intensity exercise and should not be generalized to universal endurance performance or used to attribute effects from beta-alanine plus creatine trials to beta-alanine monotherapy.
submissions.populationContext: Three hundred thirty-one trained males aged 18 to 40 years across 18 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled studies.
submissions.usageContext: Chronic beta-alanine supplementation evaluated during maximal or supramaximal exercise efforts lasting 0.5 to 10 minutes; monotherapy evidence must remain separate from beta-alanine plus creatine co-supplementation.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The pooled effect was modest and the included evidence was restricted by sex, age, training status, exercise intensity, duration, and supplementation protocol. Dose or paresthesia guidance requires separate source-specific receipts. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A placebo-controlled crossover trial found no menopausal-symptom or measured hormone benefit from topical wild-yam extract cream in postmenopausal women.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial in 23 symptomatic postmenopausal women compared topical wild-yam extract cream with placebo for three months per treatment period. Wild yam did not differ significantly from placebo for menopausal symptoms and did not produce meaningful changes in estradiol, serum or salivary progesterone, follicle-stimulating hormone, glucose, lipids, or blood pressure. This topical negative trial does not support claims that wild yam acts as progesterone in humans or reliably treats menopausal symptoms.
submissions.populationContext: Twenty-three symptomatic postmenopausal women in a double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trial.
submissions.usageContext: Topical wild-yam extract cream for three months per period; findings must not be generalized to oral extracts or other preparations.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The trial was small and tested a topical preparation. Diosgenin can be used as an industrial precursor for steroid synthesis, but that chemical manufacturing relationship does not establish conversion of wild yam or diosgenin into progesterone by the human body. The null trial does not prove every preparation is inactive. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: Poison-center intoxication cases involving Acorus calamus products documented prolonged vomiting and analytical detection of alpha- and beta-asarone in several patients.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A bioanalytical investigation reported that the Swedish Poisons Information Centre received inquiries concerning about 30 intentional intoxications with Acorus calamus products from 2003 through 2006. Urine from seven cases was analyzed: alpha-asarone was detected in five samples and beta-asarone in four, and prolonged vomiting lasting more than 15 hours was the main reported clinical symptom. The study supports a human intoxication safety signal for the products involved but does not establish population incidence, dose-response, or safety of every calamus chemotype or preparation.
submissions.populationContext: Intentional Acorus calamus product intoxication reports to a Swedish poison center; seven cases had urine samples available for analytical investigation.
submissions.safetyContext: Human observational intoxication evidence with analytical detection of asarone isomers in several cases; product composition, intent, dose, and chemotype limit generalization.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: This is a poison-center/bioanalytical case investigation rather than a controlled safety study. It cannot quantify routine-use risk or establish that all calamus preparations contain the same asarone profile. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A 2021 toxicology review concluded that human efficacy and safety of asarones remain unknown despite multiple preclinical toxicity signals and regulatory restrictions on beta-asarone-containing preparations.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2021 critical toxicological review of alpha-, beta-, and gamma-asarone noted that efficacy and safety in humans remain unknown. The reviewed toxicology literature described cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, reproductive toxicity, mutagenicity, and carcinogenicity for propenylic asarone isomers with varying evidentiary reliability, and authorities have restricted or recommended limits for beta-asarone and Acorus calamus preparations. These preclinical and regulatory concerns support a high-caution research gap but must not be converted into human incidence estimates.
submissions.usageContext: Toxicological and regulatory context for asarone isomers found in Acorus calamus; chemotype and constituent content matter.
submissions.safetyContext: Human safety remains insufficiently characterized; preclinical toxicity and regulatory restrictions warrant conservative framing without claiming known clinical incidence.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The review emphasizes sparse and variably reliable toxicological data and explicitly states that human efficacy and safety are not established. Individual asarone isomers and calamus preparations are not interchangeable. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A four-RCT meta-analysis found selected metabolic and lipid signals for a fixed Berberis aristata plus Silybum marianum product, but the evidence was limited and cannot establish Berberis monotherapy efficacy.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A systematic review and meta-analysis pooled four randomized placebo-controlled trials totaling 491 adults with dyslipidemia who received a fixed Berberis aristata plus Silybum marianum combination. The combination significantly lowered LDL cholesterol, total cholesterol, fasting plasma glucose, and HOMA index versus placebo, while HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, and body mass index were not significantly changed after three months. The authors characterized the supporting evidence as very limited and the optimal dose and duration as unclear. Because the intervention was a fixed two-plant product, these effects cannot be attributed to Berberis aristata alone or used to validate a generic Grade A herb claim.
submissions.populationContext: Four randomized placebo-controlled trials totaling 491 adults with dyslipidemia.
submissions.usageContext: Fixed Berberis aristata plus Silybum marianum combination product for three months; not Berberis aristata monotherapy and not equivalent to isolated berberine.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Combination attribution, limited trial count, unclear optimal dose/duration, and mixed endpoints materially constrain inference. The current zero-source Grade A Berberis profile is not independently validated by this staging finding. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A small randomized cancer-cachexia trial tested isolated Atractylodes lactone I rather than whole Atractylodes macrocephala, with selected positive and null outcomes.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A randomized trial in 64 cachectic cancer patients compared isolated lactone I from Atractylodes macrocephala with fish-oil-enriched nutritional supplementation. Appetite and mid-arm muscle circumference, along with selected cytokine and proteolysis-inducing-factor measures, favored the lactone-I group, while body weight and serum IL-6 were not significantly different between groups. Because the intervention was an isolated constituent rather than the whole herb, these findings cannot establish efficacy of generic Atractylodes macrocephala preparations.
submissions.populationContext: Sixty-four cachectic cancer patients randomized between isolated Atractylodes lactone I and fish-oil-enriched nutritional supplementation.
submissions.usageContext: Isolated lactone I constituent evidence in cancer cachexia; not whole-rhizome or generic botanical evidence.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The trial was small, used an active nutritional comparator, measured multiple clinical and biomarker outcomes, and tested an isolated constituent. Positive appetite/MAMC and biomarker findings must remain paired with null body-weight and IL-6 results. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A comprehensive 2021 review notes that direct clinical studies supporting Atractylodes macrocephala safety in humans are lacking despite relatively reassuring preclinical toxicity observations.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A 2021 comprehensive review of Atractylodes macrocephala summarized animal acute-toxicity, cytotoxicity, genetic-toxicity, pharmacology, and traditional-use literature and stated that clinical studies directly supporting safety in humans are lacking. The review noted an absence of serious adverse events in the limited available information, but this does not substitute for preparation-specific controlled human safety evidence or justify broad interaction claims.
submissions.usageContext: Whole-herb safety evidence gap; preclinical toxicity observations and historical/clinical-use reports do not establish controlled human safety.
submissions.safetyContext: Direct human safety evidence is insufficient; current safety and interaction language should remain conservative until preparation-specific clinical receipts exist.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: The source is a broad narrative review and much of the safety evidence is preclinical. Absence of reported serious events is not proof of safety, and findings for isolated constituents, injected extracts, mixtures, or animal studies are not interchangeable with routine oral whole-herb use. Source-registry admission and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.

submissions.findingTextShort: A five-patient case series describes sedation and perceptual disturbances after use of marketed blue-lotus products by vaping or infused beverage.
submissions.findingTextNormalized: A published case series described five active-duty patients presenting with altered mental status after using marketed blue-lotus products: four after vaping and one after an infused beverage. Sedation and perceptual disturbances were common, and all patients were managed with supportive care without sedating agents. The case series supports a route- and product-specific toxicity signal but does not establish dose-response, incidence, product authenticity, or safety of all Nymphaea caerulea preparations.
submissions.populationContext: Five active-duty patients presenting for acute altered mental status after use of marketed blue-lotus products.
submissions.usageContext: Four vaping exposures and one infused-beverage exposure; marketed product evidence rather than controlled administration of a chemically verified botanical preparation.
submissions.safetyContext: Supports conservative CNS-active safety framing and avoidance of assuming inhaled/vaped and oral products are equivalent.
submissions.uncertaintyNote: Small uncontrolled case series with uncertain product composition and no incidence denominator. It cannot establish typical-use risk, causality for every preparation, or efficacy. The paper is already represented in the current profile and is staged here to create a bounded claim-level safety finding rather than as net-new literature. Source-registry and semantic citation attestation remain required before promotion.
